titleEn: Cast your burden on the LORD
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A | Dm Dm |
intro: Twenty-four verses of a man being destroyed by someone he used to pray beside. The first movement is panic and a wish for wings; the second is a city patrolled by its own corruption; the hinge is verse 14, where the enemy is finally identified as a friend; the last third is a decision to trust taken without any report that the situation improved. In the cycle that reads the whole book across thirty days it falls on the tenth. Grammatically it is a good place to meet the cohortative, the I would form ending in -a: verses 7 to 9 give you I would fly, I would settle, I would hurry.

stichs.en: For the leader, with stringed instruments.
A maskil of David.

verses.summary: The heading gives the scoring and the genre before any trouble is named. A maskil is a psalm marked for instruction, so what follows is meant to teach and not only to vent.

stichs.en: Give ear, God, to my prayer,
and do not hide Yourself from my plea.

verses.summary: The first request is not for rescue but for attention. The negative half asks God not to do the one thing the psalm fears, which is to withdraw and go quiet.

stichs.en: Attend to me and answer me;
I am restless in my complaint, and I moan,

verses.summary: Three imperatives in a row, then the reason. The speaker admits he is not composed: the verb of complaint is followed by a verb for the noise an animal makes.

stichs.en: because of the voice of an enemy, in the face of pressure from a wicked man;
for they tip trouble onto me, and in anger they hound me.

glosses: they bear a grudge against me
verses.summary: The cause arrives only now, and it is sound before it is action: a voice, then pressure, then something dropped from above onto the speaker.

stichs.en: My heart writhes inside me,
and the terrors of death have fallen on me.

verses.summary: The damage has moved indoors. Heart first, then the terrors of death, and the direction of both is toward the speaker rather than away from him.

stichs.en: Fear and trembling enter me,
and shuddering has covered me.

verses.summary: Four words of panic in six. The last verb makes the fear a garment, something that goes over a person completely rather than striking one part of him.

stichs.en: And I said: who will give me a wing like a dove?
I would fly away and settle.

verses.summary: The escape fantasy begins, and it is specific: not strength, not a weapon, wings. What he wants is not to win but to be somewhere else.

stichs.en: See, I would wander far off,
I would spend the night in the wilderness. Selah.

verses.summary: The dove flight acquires a destination. The wilderness is chosen for the one thing it reliably offers, which is that nobody else is in it.

stichs.en: I would hurry to find myself a refuge
from the driving wind, from the storm.

verses.summary: The fantasy ends on weather. Wind and storm are how the psalm names a human situation it is not yet willing to describe directly.

stichs.en: Swallow them up, Lord; split their tongue,
for I have seen violence and strife in the city.

verses.summary: The prayer turns hostile, and what it asks for is confusion of speech, which is the one thing a city held together by plotting cannot survive.

stichs.en: Day and night they circle it on its walls,
and iniquity and trouble are inside it.

verses.summary: The city is patrolled, but by the wrong thing. What goes round the walls is not a watch keeping harm out, it is the harm itself.

stichs.en: Ruin is inside it,
and oppression and deceit never leave its public square.

verses.summary: The square is where business is done and disputes are judged in public. Naming it as the place the corruption never leaves says the institutions are gone, not only the people.

stichs.en: For it is not an enemy who taunts me, then I could bear it;
it is not one who hates me who rose over me, then I could hide from him.

verses.summary: The hardest verse here to construe, and the argument runs on two conditions: an enemy would have been survivable, because an enemy is a thing you can see coming and avoid.

stichs.en: But it is you, a man of my own rank,
my companion, the one I knew.

verses.summary: The accusation lands. Three terms of closeness stacked in five words, and the pronoun opening the verse is the emphatic one, which is what makes the sentence a wound.

stichs.en: who with me made confidence sweet;
in the house of God we walked among the crowd.

verses.summary: The betrayal is dated to a shared past, and the setting is worship. Private counsel and public procession, both lost in one line.

stichs.en: Let death come upon them,
let them go down alive to Sheol,
for evil is where they live, and inside them.

verses.summary: The curse. It asks the ground to open on people who are still walking about, which is this psalm's way of saying the rot has already finished its work.

stichs.en: As for me, I call to God,
and the LORD will save me.

verses.summary: The turn. Nothing in the situation has changed and nothing is claimed to have changed; what moves is the direction the speaker is facing.

stichs.en: Evening and morning and noon I complain and moan,
and He has heard my voice.

verses.summary: Three fixed times, and the two verbs of verse 3 come back unchanged. What is new is the last clause: the same noise, now reported as received.

stichs.en: He has ransomed my soul in peace from the battle against me,
for they were many, ranged with me.

verses.summary: A rescue reported in the perfect tense while the danger is still being described as numerous. The last two words are the hardest in the psalm to settle.

stichs.en: God will hear and will answer them, He who is enthroned from of old. Selah.
Those who have no changes,
and do not fear God.

verses.summary: The counterweight to the enemy's confidence. The charge laid against them is not cruelty but never having been altered by anything that happened to them.

stichs.en: He put out his hands against those at peace with him;
he profaned his covenant.

glosses: against those at peace with him
verses.summary: Back to the friend, and now in the third person. Hands go out against people who were at peace with him, which is the whole definition of the crime.

stichs.en: Smoother than butter was his mouth,
but his heart was war;
his words were softer than oil,
yet they were drawn swords.

verses.summary: Four images, all of them about texture. Soft speech is set against a heart that is a battlefield, and the last word turns the words themselves into blades.

stichs.en: Cast what is given you onto the LORD,
and He will sustain you.
He will never let the righteous be shaken.

verses.summary: The one line of this psalm most people know. It is aimed outward at the reader, and it is the only imperative in the psalm addressed to a human being.

stichs.en: But You, God, will bring them down to the pit of destruction;
men of blood and deceit will not reach half their days.
But I will trust in You.

verses.summary: Two futures set beside each other, and the psalm ends on the shorter of the two sentences. The final word is the pronoun for God.

pardes.body: Three movements. Verses 2 to 9 are distress and end in a fantasy of escape: wings, wilderness, a shelter from a storm. Verses 10 to 16 turn to the city and find the danger inside the walls, where it has a face and a name. Verses 17 to 24 are a decision to trust, taken with no report that anything outside the speaker got better. The hinge is {{14.0}}, an emphatic pronoun put first in its clause: up to that point the trouble is an enemy, from there it is a friend. Note that the escape is never taken. The dove flight is stated as a wish and then dropped without comment.

The consonants q-r-b run through the psalm in two senses the ear cannot separate. Inside: my heart writhes inside me in verse 5, inside her in verses 11 and 12, inside them in verse 16. Combat: {{22.3}}, his heart was war, and {{19.3}}, from the battle against me. A psalm about what is inside a person is built on the word for close fighting. Two readings stay unsettled and this page does not settle them. The first word of verse 16, {{16.0}}, is written one way and read another in the Masoretic tradition, and translations divide between a verb, may He incite death against them, and a reading built on a noun for desolation; it is disputed. The last word of verse 19, {{19.8}}, plainly means with me, which is why some render for they were many against me and others for many were on my side, and the verse can be read either as rescue from a crowd or as rescue by one.

Traditional commentary identifies the friend of verses 14 and 15 with Ahithophel, David's counsellor, who went over to Absalom's revolt in 2 Samuel 15 to 17 and whose advice the book says was treated like an oracle. On that reading the shared walk to the house of God is not a general memory of friendship but a working relationship inside the court. Verse 18 names three times of prayer, evening and morning and noon, in that order, and the same three times appear in Daniel 6:11; the pair is a fixture in discussions of why the day carries three fixed prayers. One structural detail is worth holding onto: {{23.0}} is the only imperative in twenty-four verses that is addressed to a person rather than to God.

The psalm uses two divine names and does not scatter them at random. The name read as God carries the appeals of verses 2 and 17 and the judgment of verse 24; the four letter name appears at the moment of rescue in verse 17 and in the instruction of verse 23. In the standard reading of the two names, one is strict measure and the other is mercy, so the psalm crosses from the first to the second while the circumstances stay exactly as they were. The wilderness of verse 8 is read in this key not as flight from the world but as the place where nothing stands between a person and the source, which is why the wish is answered in a form the speaker did not ask for: the shelter arrives, the wings do not.
